newsitem.title: USA: Rock Hall of Fame enshrines glittery lineup.
newsitem.headline: Rock Hall of Fame enshrines glittery lineup.

text.p: A roll call of pop music heavyweights -- including the Jackson Five, Bee Gees, and Crosby, Stills and Nash -- will take their place in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame on Tuesday.

Organisers of the event said they expected most of this year's inductees to appear and perform on Tuesday night in a one-of-a-kind concert and ceremony in a downtown hotel where the few hundred seats made available to the public were long ago snatched up at $1,250 each.

The 1996 ceremonies were the first held in Cleveland, home of the $100 million glass and steel Rock and Roll Hall of Fame perched on the edge of Lake Erie. The ceremonies had been in New York City since inductions began in 1986, except for 1993 when the event moved to Los Angeles.
This year's lineup salutes folk and rock harmonies and celebrates Motown, disco, soul and funk. The inductees:

-- The Bee Gees, consisting of the three Gibb brothers, 49-year-old twins Maurice and Robin and Barry, 47. The honour came on the day their new album, "Still Water," already winning raves in Europe, was released in the United States. The disco beat typified by their 1977 "Saturday Night Fever" soundtrack is again luring fans to the dance floor.

-- Buffalo Springfield, which lasted only from 1966 to 1968 but paved the way for what became country rock. The group, whose "For What It's Worth" caught the anti-establishment fever of the time, featured guitarists Stephen Stills, Neil Young and Richie Furay, bassist Bruce Palmer and drummer Dewey Martin. Producer, singer and songwriter Jim Messina later replaced Palmer.

-- Crosby, Stills and Nash, which began in 1968 when Stills joined Graham Nash and David Crosby in a blend of rich harmonies and near perfect musical technique. Their first album was a sensation in 1969, and Young later joined the group from time to time.

-- The Jackson Five, which featured then 11-year-old Michael Jackson, took the Motown sound to a new level at the end of the 1960s. A superstar for years and now 38, Michael was joined by brothers Jackie, 47, Tito, 45, Jermaine, 42, and Marlon, 40.

-- Joni Mitchell, 53, the nightingale-voiced Canadian folk singer and songwriter who put out her first album in 1967 and provided a steady stream of songs for other artists. Her often unique guitar tunings, the result of a polio-weakened left hand, led to chords that sometimes moved beyond folk to jazz.

-- George Clinton, the New Jersey-born king of funk and father of Parliament and Funkadelic, the two groups inducted along with him. Clinton heavily influenced a broad range of new artists like Prince and the Red Hot Chili Peppers.

-- The (Young) Rascals, who came together in New York City in 1964 and became one of the industry's premier "blue-eyed soul" groups. Singer-organist Felix Cavaliere, guitarist Gene Cornish, vocalist Edie Brigati and drummer Dino Danelli had chart-topping hits with "Good Lovin'" and "Groovin'" in 1966 and 1967.

Also enshrined as early influences will be the late bluegrass king Bill Monroe, late gospel great Mahalia Jackson, and Cincinnati record producer Syd Nathan, founder of the King Records label who gave James Brown and others their starts.

A nominating committee begins the election process by selecting candidates, all of whom must have cut their first record at least 25 years earlier. About 1,000 rock experts from around the world elect the inductees.

Those named to the hall are commemorated in a special space at the museum. Of the living inductees, only Young and Mitchell did not plan to attend Tuesday's ceremonies, which were available live on the Internet at www.rockhall.com.
